newsitem.title: UK: UK Sea Empress oil spill blamed on avoidable fault.
newsitem.headline: UK Sea Empress oil spill blamed on avoidable fault.

text.p: Poor training of pilots, poor communications and unnecessary bureaucracy were to blame for one of Britain's worst oil spills when a tanker spilt 72,000 tonnes of oil off the south Welsh coast, a leaked government report was quoted as saying on Friday.
The British Broadcasting Corporation quoted the draft report into the Sea Empress disaster last February as saying waters at the entrance of Milford Haven harbour were not properly charted.

It also said the official salvage team did not realise it could have got the grounded Liberian-flagged tanker into port two days after the accident because it was given inaccurate information about tides.
A "breakdown of communication" led to the spillage, which could have been limited to 2,000 tonnes if the crisis had been better handled, the report said.
"The standards of training and examination of pilots at Milford Haven are unsatisfactory and in need of improvement," the BBC quoted the Marine Accident Investigation Branch as saying.

A Department of Transport spokesman declined to comment in detail. But he said a draft report had been "circulated to all people whose reputations may be adversely affected by the report" in early December, and that it would be published in one or two months.
The BBC said the draft report also blamed the spill from the 147,000 dwt tanker, built in 1993, on "time-consuming and unnecessary bureaucratic procedures."
The Coastguard Agency said this week that the cleanup operation "was a most successful cooperation between central government, local authorities and the port authority."

The Coastguard's Marine Pollution Control Unit said that "thanks to aerial spraying of dispersants and recovery of some oil at sea only some 3,000-5,000 tonnes of oil reached the shoreline." Allowing for evaporation, there had been a potential 43,000 tonnes to come ashore.
The spill caused considerable damage to local wildlife in an area with some of the most important seabird colonies in Western Europe.
